title: Reconstructive Memory
subject: psych
paras: It is natural to think of memory as a kind of recording device. On this view, an experience is stored somewhere in the brain, and remembering it is simply a matter of playing the recording back. Over the past century, however, psychologists have gathered a great deal of evidence that memory does not work this way. Instead, remembering appears to be an active process in which the mind rebuilds past events from fragments, filling in the gaps with general knowledge and expectations. Psychologists describe this view as reconstructive memory.

One of the earliest demonstrations came from the British psychologist Frederic Bartlett in the 1930s. Bartlett asked English university students to read a Native American folk tale called "The War of the Ghosts" and then to retell it after various delays. The story contained events and ideas that seemed strange to the students. In their retellings, the students shortened the story, left out details that did not make sense to them, and changed unfamiliar elements into more familiar ones; canoes, for example, sometimes became boats. Bartlett concluded that people remember events through schemas, mental frameworks built from previous experience that organize new information.

Schemas are useful because they allow people to understand and store information efficiently. [■] Someone who has eaten in many restaurants does not need to memorize every step of a new restaurant visit, since the general pattern of being seated, ordering, eating, and paying is already familiar. [■] The cost of this efficiency is that schemas can also distort memory. [■] In one study, participants who waited briefly in an office later recalled seeing books there, even though the room had contained none; books are simply what people expect to find in an office. [■]

Later research showed that memories can also be changed by information received after an event. In a famous series of experiments in the 1970s, the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed participants films of car accidents and then asked them questions about what they had seen. When participants were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other, they gave higher estimates of speed than participants who were asked how fast the cars were going when they "hit" each other. A week later, those in the "smashed" group were also more likely to report having seen broken glass, although there had been none in the film. The wording of a single question had altered their memory of the event.

These findings have serious consequences in the legal system, where the testimony of eyewitnesses has traditionally been considered very persuasive. Studies of cases in which convicted people were later cleared by DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in a large proportion of them. Witnesses in these cases were not lying; they sincerely believed their memories. As a result, many police departments have changed the way they conduct interviews and lineups, for example by avoiding leading questions and by having lineups run by officers who do not know which person is the suspect.

It would be wrong to conclude that memory is generally unreliable. In everyday life, the gist of most memories is accurate enough to guide behavior. Some researchers argue that the flexibility of memory is actually an advantage: a system that combines fragments of the past with general knowledge may also be what allows people to imagine the future and to plan for situations they have never encountered. The same processes that sometimes cause errors may therefore serve important purposes.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, the reconstructive view holds that remembering involves
opts: playing back an exact recording of an experience
rebuilding events from fragments and general knowledge
storing each experience in a separate part of the brain
forgetting all unimportant details immediately
qs.why: the mind rebuilds past events from fragments, filling in the gaps…

qs.q: The word "fragments" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
opts: small pieces
strong feelings
clear images
false ideas

qs.q: Why does the author mention that "canoes… sometimes became boats" in paragraph 2?
opts: To show that the students had poor knowledge of geography
To give an example of unfamiliar details being changed into familiar ones
To suggest that the story was translated incorrectly
To prove that the students did not read the story
qs.why: changed unfamiliar elements into more familiar ones; canoes, for example…

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, what are schemas?
opts: Stories that are passed down in a culture
Mental frameworks based on past experience that organize new information
Errors made when retelling a story
Tests used to measure memory
qs.why: schemas, mental frameworks built from previous experience that organize new information。

qs.q: Look at the four squares [■] that indicate where the following sentence could be added to paragraph 3. "When an event does not fit the expected pattern, people may unknowingly reshape it until it does." Where would the sentence best fit?
opts: After the first square
After the second square
After the third square
After the fourth square
qs.why: 放在 The cost… can also distort memory 之后，解释如何扭曲，再引出办公室里的书的例子。

qs.q: What can be inferred from the office study described in paragraph 3?
opts: Participants had read many books while waiting.
Participants' expectations led them to remember things that were not present.
The office was too dark to see clearly.
Participants intentionally gave false answers.
qs.why: books are simply what people expect to find in an office —— 期望导致错误记忆。

qs.q: According to paragraph 4, participants who heard the word "smashed" were more likely than others to
opts: say they had seen broken glass
remember the color of the cars
refuse to answer questions
forget the film entirely
qs.why: …more likely to report having seen broken glass, although there had been none。

qs.q: The word "them" in paragraph 5 ("a large proportion of them") refers to
opts: police departments
eyewitnesses
cases in which convicted people were later cleared
DNA tests
qs.why: them 指 cases in which convicted people were later cleared by DNA evidence。

qs.q: Based on paragraph 5, why would police use officers who do not know which person is the suspect to run lineups?
opts: To save time during investigations
To prevent the officers from unintentionally influencing witnesses
Because experienced officers are not available
To make witnesses feel more confident
qs.why: 与避免诱导性问题同理，防止无意中影响证人。

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: Research suggests that memory is reconstructive rather than a simple recording.
opts: Bartlett found that people reshape memories to fit schemas built from earlier experience.
Loftus showed that information received after an event, such as the wording of a question, can alter memory.
Bartlett's students were studying at English universities.
Errors in eyewitness memory have led to wrongful convictions and changes in police procedures.
Most people's memories of restaurants are completely accurate.
DNA evidence was first used in the 1930s.
qs.why: C 是细节；E、F 与原文不符。
